Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society season ticket, 1890

Walter Crane’s season ticket for the society that named the movement: a designer and a workman shake hands inside a framed woodcut-style panel.

Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A describes it as “Walter Crane. Season ticket, The Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society, 1890”, process engraving, 77 × 133 mm, given by Emslie John Horniman. V&A.

The Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society, which gave its name to the movement, was formed in 1887 with Walter Crane as president and held its first exhibition at the New Gallery, London, in November 1888. Wikipedia: Arts and Crafts movement.

Observed

  • The card is printed in one dark brown ink on cream.
  • On the left, a square panel with a double-line frame shows a young man in a tunic and a bearded workman in an apron shaking hands over a small tree, with laurel sprays and acanthus leaves behind them.
  • Banners in the panel read “THE ARTS & CRAFTS EXHIBITION SOCIETY”, and ribbons at the foot read “121. REGENT ST.” and “·THE·NEW·GALLERY·”.
  • A vertical rule divides the panel from the right half, where “·SEASON· ·TICKET· ·1890·”, “ADMIT”, and “DURING THE PERIOD OF THE EXHIBITION ERNEST RADFORD SECRETARY” are hand-drawn in capitals with middle dots between words.
  • A dotted box leaves space for the holder’s name. “A&CES” is written at the lower left.

Why it belongs

The ticket confirms the framed panel and the double-rule frame of the rubric, but all its lettering is capitals. The style’s hand lettering is often capitals with middle dots, not mixed case.

The one-colour brown print is a cheaper, reproductive version of the Kelmscott look, useful as a model for small formats.

Borrow

Separate words in a capital heading with middle dots (·) instead of spacing them out.

Divide a card into a framed picture panel and a lettered text half with a single vertical rule.
